newsitem.title: POLAND: Britain pushes Poland trade, voices complaints.
newsitem.headline: Britain pushes Poland trade, voices complaints.

text.p: British Trade Minister Anthony Nelson singled out Poland on Friday as a key to his country's new campaign to boost trade and investment in central Europe, but complained that Poland was unfair to spirits exporters.

Nelson spent the day in Warsaw promoting an "Open for Business" project launched in London this week and was to meet Poland's European integration chief Danuta Huebner and Economy Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek.
He said among other topics he would raise the issue of restraints on bilateral trade, notably on spirits and tobacco.
"Britain is disappointed that Poland has retained quotas on imports of spirits," Nelson told a news conference.
Poland sets a quota for imports of foreign spirits, above which it levies a tariff of 344 percent.

Within this quota, which is seldom exceeded, it levies an 85 percent duty, plus further payments according to the strength of the alcohol, excise tax, value added tax and retail and wholesale margins which are set by the government. @

"This means that a bottle of Johnny Walker Red Label (whisky) in the Czech Republic costs $15 and in Poland $30," John Harrod, External Affairs Manager of United Distillers (Poland), part of Guinness Plc, told reporters.

Nelson said the 85 percent duty within the quota was very high and the non-quota rate of 344 percent deterred increased trade and should have been abolished under Poland's agreement with the European Union which it aims to join soon.
"I think this gives a disappointing signal on EU integration and we intend to raise this in the EU-Poland association committee in March," Nelson said.
He said Britain was also concerned over Polish excise duty and VAT structures for cigarettes, which might undermine investment plans of tobacco firms.
But Nelson said these issues should not cloud his message that Poland was a good market for Britain.

He said bilateral trade between the two countries exceeded $3 billion a year and was growing by about 40 percent a year, while British investments in Poland, current or in the pipeline, were worth about $1 billion.
He said the new trade promotion would aim largely to lure small and medium sized enterprises to Poland, which had so far sometimes seen it as a difficult and distant market.

The British Department of Trade and Industry's 18-month campaign, also aimed at the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia and Slovenia, aims to create 100 investment projects and double Britain's exports to the region to $4 billion by 1998.
